title: Case Types and Stages
learning_objectives: Understand what case types are and their purpose
Learn how to design effective case stages

introduction.title: Understanding Case Types and Stages
introduction.text: Case types and stages are fundamental concepts in PEGA that define the structure and lifecycle of your business processes. A case type represents a category of work, while stages represent the major phases that work progresses through. Understanding how to design and configure these elements is crucial for building effective PEGA applications.

sections.title: What are Case Types?
sections.content: A case type is a template that defines the structure, behavior, and lifecycle of a specific category of work in your organization. Think of it as a blueprint that determines how similar pieces of work will be handled.
key_points: Case types define the structure and behavior of work units
Each case type has its own lifecycle and business rules
Case types can inherit from other case types
They include data fields, processes, and user interfaces

examples.description: Handles customer service inquiries and support requests
Manages the procurement process from request to fulfillment
Guides new employee setup and orientation process

sections.title: Understanding Case Stages
sections.content: Case stages represent the major phases or milestones in a case's lifecycle. They provide a high-level view of where a case stands and help organize the work into logical groupings.

stage_characteristics.description: Cases typically move through stages in a logical sequence, though some stages may be skipped or repeated based on business rules.
Stages serve as major milestones that help track progress and provide visibility into case status.
Each stage contains related processes and activities that need to be completed before moving to the next stage.
Stages should reflect meaningful business phases that stakeholders can easily understand and relate to.

sections.title: Designing Effective Case Stages
sections.content: Good stage design is crucial for creating intuitive and efficient case management processes. Here are key principles for designing effective stages.

design_principles.description: Use stage names that clearly communicate the business purpose and are easily understood by all stakeholders.
Group related activities and processes within the same stage to maintain coherence and efficiency.
design_principles.example: In a loan application, group all verification activities (income, credit, employment) in a 'Verification' stage rather than spreading them across multiple stages.

design_principles.description: Define clear conditions for when a case enters and exits each stage.
design_principles.example: A case enters 'Review' stage when all required documents are submitted, and exits when approval decision is made.

design_principles.description: Balance between too many stages (overwhelming) and too few stages (not enough visibility).
design_principles.recommendation: Typically 3-7 stages work well for most business processes.

sections.title: Configuring Case Stages in PEGA
sections.content: PEGA provides powerful tools for configuring case stages with various properties and behaviors.

configuration_options.description: Basic stage configuration including name, description, and display settings.
Rules that determine when a case can enter a particular stage.
Rules that determine when a case can leave a stage and move to the next.
The workflows and activities that occur within each stage.
components: Primary processes that must be completed
Optional processes that may be triggered

sections.title: Stage Transitions and Flow Control
sections.content: Understanding how cases move between stages is crucial for designing smooth and efficient processes.

transition_types.description: Cases move to the next stage automatically when exit conditions are met.
use_cases: When all required data is collected

transition_types.description: Users explicitly move cases to the next stage through user actions.
Cases move to different stages based on business conditions or data values.
use_cases: High-value cases go to special review
Different product types follow different paths

sections.title: Best Practices for Case Types and Stages
sections.content: Follow these best practices to create effective and maintainable case type designs.

practices: Start with the business process, not the technology
Involve business stakeholders in stage design
Keep stage names business-friendly and intuitive
Design for the most common scenarios first
Plan for exceptions and edge cases
Use consistent naming conventions across case types
Document stage purposes and criteria clearly
Regularly review and optimize stage design
Gather feedback from users and stakeholders
Monitor case metrics and identify improvements
Plan for future enhancements and changes

sections.title: Common Stage Design Patterns
sections.content: Learn from common patterns that work well across different types of business processes.

patterns.description: Cases move through stages in a fixed sequence from start to finish.
patterns.example: Employee Onboarding: Application → Background Check → Documentation → Training → Completion
patterns.when_to_use: Simple, predictable processes with clear sequential steps

patterns.description: Multiple activities occur simultaneously in the same stage or across different stages.
patterns.example: Loan Processing: Credit Check and Income Verification happen simultaneously
patterns.when_to_use: When independent activities can be done concurrently to save time

patterns.description: Cases follow different paths based on data values or business conditions.
patterns.example: Insurance Claims: Simple claims go to Auto-Processing, Complex claims go to Manual Review
patterns.when_to_use: When different types of cases require different handling approaches

patterns.description: Cases can return to previous stages for corrections or additional work.
patterns.example: Document Review: Draft → Review → Rework (if needed) → Approval
patterns.when_to_use: When quality control or iterative refinement is required

summary.title: Key Takeaways
points: Case types define the structure and behavior of work categories
Stages represent major phases in a case's lifecycle
Good stage design uses business-meaningful names and logical grouping
Entry and exit conditions control stage transitions
Different transition types serve different business needs
Common patterns can guide effective stage design

next_steps.title: What's Next?
next_steps.text: Now that you understand case types and stages, you can explore more advanced topics like user interface design and data validation to create complete, user-friendly applications.
